hook_text: Throw a ball straight up. At the very top, its speed is zero — so is its acceleration zero too?
clip_script: Throw a ball straight up at 19,6 metres per second and watch gravity run the simplest tax system on Earth: every second, it takes 9,8 off your speed. After one second you're doing 9,8. After two — nothing. The ball hangs at the top of its flight, perfectly still for an instant. Now the exam question that catches thousands of matrics: at that moment, is the acceleration zero too? No. The tax collector doesn't go home just because your account hits zero. The acceleration is 9,8 metres per second squared, downward, the entire flight — going up, at the top, coming down. And because the tax rate never changes, the trip back down is the trip up played in reverse: two seconds up, two seconds down, and the ball lands in your hand at exactly 19,6 — the same speed you threw it with. Time up equals time down. Speed at any height going up equals speed at that height coming down. Know half the story and physics gives you the other half free. That symmetry, plus three equations, is the whole topic — the most predictable question in Paper 1.
visual_style: A ball rising in slow motion with a shrinking speed counter beside it, freezing at the top with a bold 'v = 0, a = 9,8' stamp, then the footage literally playing in reverse as the counter climbs back to 19,6.
mood: Calm and confident — a trick question defused in real time.
pacing: Steady climb with the counter, dramatic freeze at the top, satisfying mirrored descent, quick close.
